==Problem==
What is the correct ordering of the three numbers <imath> \frac{5}{19} </imath>, <imath> \frac{7}{21} </imath>, and <imath> \frac{9}{23} </imath>, in increasing order?

<imath> \textbf{(A)}\hspace{.05in}\frac{9}{23}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{5}{19}\quad\textbf{(B)}\hspace{.05in}\frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}\quad\textbf{(C)}\hspace{.05in}\frac{9}{23}<\frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21} </imath> 

<imath> \textbf{(D)}\hspace{.05in}\frac{5}{19}<\frac{9}{23}<\frac{7}{21}\quad\textbf{(E)}\hspace{.05in}\frac{7}{21}<\frac{5}{19}<\frac{9}{23} </imath>

==Solution 1==
The value of <imath> \frac{7}{21} </imath> is <imath> \frac{1}{3} </imath>. Now we give all the fractions a common denominator.

<imath> \frac{5}{19} \implies \frac{345}{1311} </imath>

<imath> \frac{1}{3} \implies \frac{437}{1311} </imath>

<imath> \frac{9}{23} \implies \frac{513}{1311} </imath>

Ordering the fractions from least to greatest, we find that they are in the order listed. Therefore, our final answer is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}} </imath>.

==Solution 2==
Change <imath>7/21</imath> into <imath>1/3</imath>;
<cmath>\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{5}{5}=\frac{5}{15}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{5}{15}>\frac{5}{19}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{7}{21}>\frac{5}{19}</cmath>
And
<cmath>\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{9}{9}=\frac{9}{27}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{9}{27}<\frac{9}{23}</cmath>
<cmath>\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}</cmath>
Therefore,  our answer is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}} </imath>.

==Solution 3 (quick and easy)==
We know that <imath>\frac{5}{19}</imath> is <imath>\frac{14}{19}</imath> away from <imath>1</imath>, <imath>\frac{7}{21}</imath> is <imath>\frac{14}{21}</imath> away from <imath>1</imath>, and <imath>\frac{9}{23}</imath> is <imath>\frac{14}{23}</imath> away from <imath>1</imath>. Since <imath>\frac{14}{19}</imath> is the largest, we know that it is the farthest away from 0, and <imath>\frac{14}{23}</imath> is the smallest, so it is the closest to 0. Therefore,  our answer is <imath> \boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}} </imath>.

==Solution 4==

Let <imath>\frac{a}{b}<1</imath>, so <imath>b>a</imath>. We claim that <imath>\frac{a}{b}<\frac{a+2}{b+2}</imath>. Cross-multiplying gives
<imath>a(b+2)<b(a+2)\Rightarrow ab+2a<ab+2b\Rightarrow 2a<2b\Rightarrow a<b</imath>,
which is true.

Since all fractions are less than <imath>1</imath>, this applies here: and
<imath>\frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21} and \frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}</imath>.

Thus the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}}</imath>.

Note: The value <imath>2</imath> is not special, this works for any positive number. Just make sure that the fraction is less than 1 and you add it to both the numerator and denominator.

==Solution 5==
Just solve <imath>\frac{5}{19}</imath> and <imath>\frac{9}{23}</imath> to 2 or 3 decimal places, since <imath>\frac{7}{21}</imath> = <imath>\frac{1}{3}</imath>. You get <imath> 0.26 </imath> and <imath> 0.39 </imath> respectively, so, <imath>\frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}</imath> and <imath>\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}</imath>.

hence the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ \frac{5}{19}<\frac{7}{21}<\frac{9}{23}}</imath>.
